subsections.title: AI and Academic Integrity in Teaching

content.text: Navigate the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence in education responsibly, teaching students to use AI as a tool ethically while maintaining academic integrity and developing critical thinking skills.
content.title: Purpose

content.text: Appropriate Teacher Uses of AI: Lesson Planning and Resource Creation

items: Generate lesson plan drafts, discussion questions, activity ideas (always review and customize)
Create differentiated versions of texts or problems
Develop rubrics, assessment questions, example scenarios
Critical: Always fact-check AI output; AI can produce inaccurate information
content.title: 7.13.1 Teacher Use of AI

content.text: Administrative Tasks

items: Draft parent emails (personalize before sending)
Summarize meeting notes
Create data visualizations from assessment results

content.text: Professional Learning

items: Explore pedagogical strategies for specific challenges
Generate ideas for classroom management or engagement
Practice difficult conversations (AI as role-play partner)

content.text: Cautions:

items: Never input personally identifiable student information into AI tools (violates privacy)
Don't rely solely on AI; professional judgment essential
Be transparent with colleagues about AI-assisted materials

content.text: Educators must explicitly teach students about AI (capabilities, limitations, ethics, appropriate use). AI Literacy Curriculum (Integrate Across Subjects): Understanding AI Basics

items: What is AI? How does it work (simplified)?
Types of AI: Generative (ChatGPT, DALL-E), Analytical (recommendation systems), Predictive (spam filters)
Limitations: AI lacks understanding, can produce false information confidently ("hallucinations"), reflects biases in training data
content.title: 7.13.2 Teaching Students About AI

content.text: Critical Evaluation of AI Output

items: Always verify AI-generated information with credible sources
Recognize when AI gives plausible-sounding but incorrect answers
Understand that AI cannot replace human creativity, critical thinking, ethical judgment

content.text: Ethical Use of AI

items: Appropriate uses: Brainstorming, outlining, checking grammar, learning new concepts
Inappropriate uses: Submitting AI-generated work as your own, bypassing learning process, academic dishonesty
Giving credit: Cite AI use when required by assignment

content.text: AI and Society

items: Benefits: Accessibility (text-to-speech for visually impaired), efficiency, innovation
Risks: Job displacement, misinformation, privacy concerns, algorithmic bias
Responsible AI development and use

content.text: School Policy on Student AI Use: Each school should have clear AI policy outlined in Student Handbook and communicated to students/parents. Typical policy includes:

items: Permitted Uses: Brainstorming, grammar checking, understanding concepts explained by AI tutor, generating practice problems
Prohibited Uses: Submitting AI-written essays/assignments as own work without disclosure, using AI to complete assessments meant to measure individual learning
Declaration Requirement: For assignments where AI use permitted, students must declare how AI was used and cite it
content.title: 7.13.3 Detecting and Addressing AI Misuse

content.text: Detecting Potential AI Misuse (Red Flags):

items: Sudden dramatic improvement in writing quality/complexity
Vocabulary or phrasing inconsistent with student's typical work
Generic, non-specific content lacking personal voice or examples from class
Factual errors or "hallucinations" common in AI (incorrect dates, fake citations, plausible-sounding but false information)
Responses to prompts that don't fully address specific assignment requirements

content.text: Detection Tools:

items: AI detectors (Turnitin, GPTZero) have limited accuracy; use as one data point, not definitive proof
Better approach: Design assignments resistant to AI misuse (see below)

content.text: When AI Misuse Suspected:

steps: Have Conversation with Student (not accusatory; curious)

items: "Can you explain your thinking process for this part of your essay?"
"Tell me more about this source you cited—where did you find it?"
Student unable to explain their own work is strong indicator of misuse

steps: Review Evidence: Compare to previous work, check for patterns
Apply Consequences per school policy:

items: First offense: Re-do assignment with supervision, discussion on academic integrity
Repeated offenses: More serious consequences (See Student Handbook - Academic Integrity Policy)

steps: Document Incident: Record in student file; inform parents

content.text: Assignment Design to Reduce AI Misuse: Strategies:

items.text: Personalization: Require students to connect to their own experiences, observations, community
items: Example: "Write essay analyzing symbolism in Things Fall Apart and connecting themes to a current event in your own community (name specific event)."
Process-Based Assessment: Require submission of brainstorms, outlines, drafts, reflections (AI can't replicate genuine process over time)
In-Class Components: Timed writing, presentations, discussions where students must explain thinking
Specific, Unique Prompts: Avoid generic essay topics easily found online or generated by AI
Oral Defense: Students present work and answer questions about their process and choices
Multimodal: Combine written work with visual, audio, or hands-on components

subsections.title: AI Integration Policy Framework for School Leadership

content.text: Purpose Establish a comprehensive institutional framework for AI integration across Eduversal partner schools, providing school leaders with strategic guidance on implementation, resource allocation, professional development, data governance, and quality assurance. This section complements the practical classroom guidance in Section 7.13 by addressing the broader organizational and leadership dimensions of AI adoption.

content.title: 7.14.1 Strategic Planning for AI Integration
content.text:
School leaders are responsible for developing a coherent AI integration strategy aligned with Cambridge International standards, Indonesian regulatory requirements, and the school's improvement priorities.

**Key Components of an AI Integration Plan:**

content.title: Vision and Objectives
items: Articulate how AI integration supports the school's educational mission
Define specific, measurable goals for AI adoption (e.g., percentage of teachers using AI for lesson planning, student AI literacy benchmarks)
Align AI initiatives with existing school improvement plans and Cambridge quality standards

content.title: Priority Areas for Implementation
items: Phase 1: Teacher productivity tools (lesson planning, material creation, administrative tasks)
Phase 2: Assessment and feedback enhancement
Phase 3: Student-facing applications and AI literacy curriculum
Phase 4: Advanced personalization and data-driven instruction

content.title: Resource Requirements
items: Infrastructure needs (reliable internet, devices, platform subscriptions)
Budget allocation for AI tools and professional development
Technical support capacity

content.title: Timeline and Milestones
items: Realistic implementation schedule with clear checkpoints
Pilot programs before full-scale rollout
Regular review points to assess progress and adjust approach

content.title: Risk Assessment
items: Identification of potential challenges (staff resistance, technical issues, academic integrity concerns)
Mitigation strategies for each identified risk
Contingency plans for implementation setbacks

content.title: 7.14.2 Approved AI Tools and Platforms
content.text:
Schools must maintain a curated list of approved AI tools that have been vetted for educational suitability, data privacy compliance, and alignment with school values.

**Criteria for Tool Approval:**

content.title: Educational Value
items: Clear pedagogical purpose and demonstrated benefit to teaching or learning
Age-appropriateness for intended users
Alignment with Cambridge curriculum objectives

content.title: Data Privacy and Security
items: Compliance with Indonesian data protection regulations (UU PDP - Undang-Undang Pelindungan Data Pribadi)
Clear data handling policies from the provider
No requirement to input identifiable student information, or robust protection if such input is necessary
Data storage location and security measures

content.title: Reliability and Support
items: Stable platform with consistent availability
Adequate technical support from provider
Regular updates and improvement

content.title: Cost-Effectiveness
items: Reasonable pricing relative to educational benefit
Sustainable within school budget constraints
Clear licensing terms

content.text: The Eduversal network maintains a centrally approved tool list, updated termly. Schools may propose extra tools for network review. Using non-approved tools for work involving student information is prohibited.

content.title: Current Categories of Approved Tools
items: Generative AI assistants for teacher productivity
Assessment and quiz generation platforms
Language support tools for EAL students
Administrative automation tools

content.text: Specific approved tools are listed in a separate document maintained by the office of the Eduversal Chief Academic Officer and distributed to all partner schools.

content.title: 7.14.3 Data Governance and Privacy Protection
content.text:
Protecting student data is a fundamental leadership responsibility. School leaders must establish and enforce robust data governance practices.

**Core Data Protection Principles:**

content.title: Data Minimization
items: Use only the minimum necessary information in any AI application
Avoid entering detailed student information when general queries suffice
Aggregate data rather than individual records where possible

content.title: Anonymization Requirements
items: When AI analysis of student performance is needed, remove or code identifying information
Use class-level or cohort-level data rather than individual student data where feasible
Establish clear protocols for any exceptions requiring identifiable data

content.title: Consent and Transparency
items: Inform parents about AI tools used in instruction through appropriate communications
Obtain necessary consents as required by Indonesian regulations
Maintain transparency about how student data is used and protected

content.title: Secure Storage and Transmission
items: Ensure any locally stored AI-related data is properly secured
Use encrypted connections when transmitting sensitive information
Regularly audit data storage practices

content.title: Incident Response
items: Establish clear procedures for responding to suspected data breaches
Immediate reporting requirements to school leadership and Eduversal
Documentation and remediation protocols

content.title: Prohibited Data Practices
items: Entering student names, ID numbers, or photographs into public AI platforms
Sharing assessment results or academic records with non-approved AI tools
Using AI to make automated decisions about student placement or intervention without human review
Storing AI conversation logs containing student information on personal devices

content.title: 7.14.4 Professional Development Framework
content.text:
Effective AI integration requires systematic investment in staff capabilities. School leaders should implement a structured professional development program.

**AI Competency Levels:**

content.title: Foundation Level (All Teaching Staff)
items: Basic understanding of AI capabilities and limitations
Ability to use approved tools for lesson planning and material creation
Knowledge of data privacy requirements and academic integrity policies
Skills in reviewing and refining AI-generated content
Expected timeline: All staff achieve foundation level within first year of implementation

content.title: Practitioner Level (Teachers Progressing in AI Integration)
items: Advanced prompt engineering for complex instructional tasks
Integration of AI tools into differentiated instruction strategies
Use of AI for assessment development and feedback generation
Ability to guide students in responsible AI use
Expected timeline: Majority of staff achieve practitioner level within two years

content.title: Leader Level (Department Heads, Senior Teachers, Instructional Coaches)
items: Ability to mentor colleagues in effective AI integration
Skills in evaluating new AI tools for educational suitability
Capacity to lead professional development sessions on AI topics
Contribution to school and network policy development
Expected timeline: Identified teacher leaders achieve this level within 18 months

content.title: Professional Development Delivery Methods
items: Network-wide training sessions coordinated by the office of the Eduversal Chief Academic Officer
School-based professional learning communities focused on AI integration
Online self-directed learning modules and resources
Peer observation and collaborative planning sessions
External workshops and conferences where appropriate

content.title: Documentation and Recognition
items: keep records of staff participation in AI professional development
Include AI competency development in teacher appraisal discussions
Recognize and celebrate effective AI integration practices
Create opportunities for skilled teachers to share expertise across the network

content.title: 7.14.5 Quality Assurance and Monitoring
content.text:
School leaders must establish mechanisms to monitor AI integration quality and ensure alignment with educational objectives.

**Classroom Observation Focus Areas:**

When observing lessons involving AI integration, observers should consider:

content.title: Pedagogical Purpose
items: Is AI being used to enhance specific learning objectives?
Does AI use align with the lesson's educational goals?
Is there clear value added by AI integration?

content.title: Quality of Implementation
items: Has AI-generated content been appropriately reviewed and refined?
Is the teacher exercising professional judgment in AI use?
Are students engaging meaningfully with learning, not passively consuming AI output?

content.title: Student Learning Impact
items: Are students developing understanding and skills, not just receiving AI-generated answers?
Is AI supporting differentiation for diverse learner needs?
Are students being taught to critically evaluate AI-assisted work?

content.text:
Observation feedback should address AI integration constructively, recognizing effective practices and identifying areas for growth.

**School-Level Monitoring:**

content.title: Regular Review Meetings
items: Termly discussion of AI integration progress at leadership meetings
Department-level sharing of effective practices and challenges
Student and parent feedback collection and analysis

content.title: Data Collection
items: Track professional development participation and competency progression
Monitor academic integrity incidents related to AI
Gather teacher self-assessment data on AI integration confidence and frequency

content.title: Annual Review
items: full review of AI integration progress against strategic plan
Analysis of impact on teacher workload and student outcomes
Recommendations for policy and practice adjustments

content.title: Network-Level Quality Assurance
items: Eduversal school appraisal visits will include AI integration as an observation focus
Cross-school sharing of effective practices through principal meetings and network forums
Annual network report on AI integration progress and recommendations

content.title: 7.14.6 Equity and Inclusion in AI Integration
content.text:
AI integration must support equitable access to quality education for all students. School leaders are responsible for ensuring AI benefits reach all learners.

**Access Equity:**

content.title: Infrastructure Equity
items: Ensure reliable internet and appropriate devices are available for all classes
Prioritize resource allocation to address gaps in access
Provide in-school access for students without home technology resources

content.title: Teacher Capacity Equity
items: Support all teachers in developing AI competencies, not only early adopters
Provide extra support for teachers who find technology integration challenging
Ensure professional development is accessible to all staff

content.title: Student Opportunity Equity
items: Monitor whether AI-enhanced instruction reaches all student groups equally
Address any emerging gaps in AI-related learning opportunities
Ensure extracurricular AI activities are accessible to diverse students

content.text: **Supporting Diverse Learners:**

content.title: English as Extra Language Students
items: Leverage AI tools for vocabulary development, translation support, and language scaffolding
Use AI to create differentiated reading materials at appropriate language levels
Ensure AI integration does not disadvantage students still developing English proficiency

content.title: Students with Special Educational Needs

items: Train staff to recognize potential bias in AI-generated content

content.title: 7.14.7 Communication and Community Engagement

Effective AI integration requires clear communication with all stakeholders.

**Parent and Guardian Communication:**

subsections.title: Managing Student Behavior and Positive Discipline

content.text: Create safe, respectful, and productive learning environments through proactive behavior management, culturally responsive discipline, and restorative practices that build student accountability and relationships.
content.title: Purpose

content.text: Establish Clear Expectations from Day One

items.text: Collaboratively develop classroom norms with students (ownership increases buy-in)
items: Example norms: "Respect each other's ideas," "One person speaks at a time," "Arrive on time with materials," "Mistakes are opportunities to learn"
Post norms visibly; refer to them regularly
Teach behavioral expectations explicitly, not just state them
Model what "active listening" looks like; practice transitions
content.title: 7.15.1 Proactive Behavior Management

content.text: Build Positive Relationships

items: Greet students at door; use names; make eye contact
Show interest in students' lives beyond academics
2x10 Strategy: Spend 2 minutes per day for 10 days in a row talking with a challenging student about their interests (builds relationship, reduces behavior issues)
Recognize that behavior often communicates unmet needs (tired, hungry, anxious, confused, seeking attention/belonging)

content.text: Engaging Instruction = Less Misbehavior

items: Bored, confused, or unchallenged students misbehave more
Vary activities (no more than 10-15 minutes on one activity for younger students)
Active learning strategies keep students engaged
Clear learning goals help students understand purpose of work

content.text: Routines and Structure

items: Consistent routines for entering class, transitions, distributing materials, submitting work, leaving class
Routines reduce chaos and provide security, especially for EAL students and students with SEN
Practice routines until automatic

content.text: Positive Reinforcement

items: Catch students doing things right: "I notice the whole group is collaborating respectfully—great job!"
Specific praise: "Maria, your thoughtful question pushed our discussion deeper" (not just generic "good job")
Public praise, private correction (don't embarrass students in front of peers)

content.text: When misbehavior occurs (and it will—normal part of adolescence), respond calmly, consistently, and respectfully. Least Invasive to Most Invasive Responses (Graduated Approach): Level 1: Non-Verbal Interventions (for minor off-task behavior)

items: Proximity: Move near student; stand nearby while teaching
Eye contact: Brief look communicating "I see you; refocus"
Gesture: Point to work, tap desk gently as reminder
Pause: Stop speaking; wait for attention before continuing
content.title: 7.15.2 Responding to Misbehavior

content.text: Level 2: Verbal Reminders (for continued off-task behavior)

items: Private, quiet redirection: Lean down, speak softly, "Let's focus on task, please"
Remind of norms: "Remember our norm: One speaker at a time"
Offer choice: "You can continue working here quietly, or move to different seat to refocus. Your choice."

content.text: Level 3: Logical Consequences (for disruptive or repeated behavior)

items: Loss of privilege related to behavior: Student misuses materials → temporarily loses access
Time-out or break: Brief removal from situation to calm down (not punitive; help student reset)
Repair harm: Student damages property → helps fix or clean; student hurts feelings → apologizes

content.text: Level 4: Referral to Leadership (for serious or persistent behavior)

items: Serious offenses: Physical aggression, defiance, bullying, unsafe behavior
Persistent issues: After documenting multiple interventions without improvement
School counselor/student support: For behavior rooted in emotional, social, or trauma-related issues

content.text: Restorative Conversations (For Relationship Harm): When student behavior hurts others, use restorative questions (not punitive lecture):

steps: What happened? (Student's perspective)
Who was affected by your actions? How?
What needs to happen to make things right?
What will you do differently next time?

content.text: Purpose: Build accountability, empathy, and repair relationships (not just punish).
Recognize Cultural Differences in Communication and Behavior:

items: Eye Contact: In some Indonesian and Muslim cultures, avoiding eye contact with authority figures is respectful (not defiant or dishonest as might be interpreted in Western contexts)
Group vs. Individual Orientation: Indonesian students may be more collectivist; public shaming especially damaging; group accountability strategies can be effective
Respect for Authority: Students may not question teachers openly, even when confused; silence ≠ agreement or understanding
content.title: 7.15.3 Culturally Responsive Discipline

content.text: Avoid Bias in Discipline:

items: Research shows students from marginalized groups disproportionately disciplined for subjective behaviors (defiance, disrespect, disruption)

items.text: Check Your Assumptions: Is this behavior actually disruptive, or just different from my cultural norms?
items: Example: Student speaking loudly with expressive gestures during group work may reflect home communication style, not disrespect
Apply discipline consistently across all students; monitor your own patterns (Who am I sending out of class most often? Why?)

content.text: Trauma-Informed Approach:

items: Some students have experienced trauma (poverty, violence, loss, displacement)
Trauma can manifest as behavioral issues (fight/flight/freeze responses, difficulty regulating emotions, hypervigilance)
Respond with compassion and structure: "I see you're struggling today. Let's take a break. When you're ready, we'll work together to solve this."

content.text: The following practices are STRICTLY PROHIBITED in all Eduversal Partner Schools:

items: Physical punishment of any kind (hitting, slapping, pulling, pushing)
Humiliation or shaming (mocking, sarcasm, name-calling, public ridicule)
Excessive or punitive tasks (writing "I will not..." 100 times, excessive homework as punishment)
Withholding meals, bathroom access, or recess (basic needs cannot be used as punishment)
Isolation for extended periods without supervision
Any punishment that violates student dignity or rights
content.title: 7.15.4 Prohibited Discipline Practices

content.text:
If You Witness Prohibited Practices: Report immediately to Principal or Academic Coordinator (See Safeguarding Policy, Section 9).

Alternatives to Punitive Discipline: Use logical consequences, restorative practices, behavior contracts, collaboration with counselor/parents, teaching replacement behaviors.

See Student Handbook for complete Behavior Management Policy and disciplinary procedures.
Recognize that teacher wellbeing directly impacts teaching quality and student outcomes. Sustainable teaching practices prevent burnout and promote long-term career satisfaction.
content.title: Purpose

content.text: Prioritize Ruthlessly

items: Not everything can be perfect; identify high-impact tasks

items.text: Use 80/20 rule: Focus on 20% of efforts that yield 80% of results
items: Example: Detailed feedback on major essay (high impact) vs. grading every homework assignment with extensive comments (lower impact—spot-check instead)

content.title: 7.16.1 Workload Management Strategies

content.text: Batch Similar Tasks

items: Grade all essays in 2-3 dedicated sessions rather than sporadically
Respond to all parent emails in one time block
Plan lessons for entire week in one planning session

content.text: Use Templates and Routines

items: Lesson plan template saves time
Email templates for common communications (parent updates, absence follow-ups)
Classroom routines reduce need for constant decisions

content.text: Collaborate and Share

items: Co-plan with colleagues (divide and conquer)
Share resources in PLCs; use what colleagues have already made
Ask for help when overwhelmed

content.text: Set Boundaries

items: Establish work hours; communicate to parents (respond to non-urgent emails within 24-48 hours during school week, not immediately)
Protect weekends for rest and family (minimum one full day without school work)
Learn to say "no" to extra commitments when at capacity

content.text: Leverage Technology Efficiently

items: Use Google Classroom/LMS to streamline assignment submission and organization
Auto-grade objective questions (multiple choice, fill-in-blank) where appropriate
Voice-to-text for comments (faster than typing)

content.text: Physical Health

items: Sleep: Aim for 7-8 hours (chronic sleep deprivation impairs judgment and patience)
Nutrition: Don't skip meals; keep healthy snacks in classroom
Exercise: Even 20-30 minutes daily reduces stress, improves mood
Hydration: Drink water throughout day (keep water bottle at desk)
content.title: 7.16.2 Self-Care and Wellbeing

content.text: Mental and Emotional Health

items: Practice stress management: Deep breathing, mindfulness, meditation (apps like Headspace, Calm)
Connect with supportive colleagues; don't isolate when struggling
Seek professional support if needed (counseling, therapy)—not a sign of weakness
Celebrate small wins; teaching is hard, and progress isn't always visible immediately

content.text: Time for Joy

items: Maintain hobbies and interests outside teaching
Spend time with family and friends
Travel, read for pleasure, create, play—whatever brings you joy
Remember your identity beyond "teacher"

content.text: School Support for Wellbeing:

items.text: Eduversal Partner Schools encouraged to provide:
items: Reasonable teaching loads (contact hours, class sizes)
Adequate planning time
Professional development on wellbeing
Access to counseling or EAP (Employee Assistance Program)
Collegial, supportive culture

content.text: When to Seek Help:

items: Persistent feelings of anxiety, depression, hopelessness
Difficulty sleeping or concentrating
Physical symptoms of stress (headaches, stomach issues, frequent illness)
Thoughts of leaving profession despite loving teaching
Feeling unable to cope with daily demands

content.text: Resources: Speak with Principal, counselor, or HR about support options. Mental health is as important as physical health.

content.title: Appendix 7-A: Teacher Appraisal Rubrics (Detailed Indicators)
content.text: The rubric set runs to approximately 24 indicators across the four appraisal domains, each written at four performance levels. It is not reproduced in full here. The sample below shows the format; every other indicator follows the same three-column structure. Teachers are expected to demonstrate Proficient (Level 3) performance across all indicators as the baseline for effective teaching.
Domain 2 - Classroom Observation, Sub-Domain 2c: Instructional Process. Indicator: Uses Questioning and Discussion Techniques.

content.title: Appendix 7-A Sample Rubric — Domain 2c: Uses Questioning and Discussion Techniques
rows: Teacher's questions are primarily low-level (recall); few students participate in discussions; teacher does not probe or scaffold responses
Questions limited to "what" and "who"; teacher accepts first answer without probing; same students answer repeatedly; minimal wait time
Teacher asks mix of low and higher-level questions but predominance still low-level; some attempt to engage multiple students
Some analysis or application questions asked; teacher occasionally probes responses ("Can you explain why?"); inconsistent wait time; 40-60% of students participate
Teacher asks varied questions (recall, analysis, evaluation); uses wait time effectively; engages most students in discussion; probes and scaffolds to deepen thinking
Balanced use of Bloom's levels; consistent 5+ second wait time; encourages student-to-student discussion; 70-85% participation; follows up on student responses to extend thinking
Teacher facilitates student-led discussions; students ask each other higher-order questions; discourse is thoughtful, respectful, and intellectually rigorous; all students engaged

Students initiate questions and challenge each other's ideas respectfully; teacher acts as facilitator, not primary questioner; genuine inquiry and debate; 90%+ participation; norms for academic discourse evident
